title: Gold Market Commentary: Making waves
gist: The World Gold Council's July 2026 commentary reports gold flat at US$4,027/oz (-7.8% y-t-d, ~25% below its 29 Jan 2026 record of US$5,405), with momentum offsetting falling breakeven inflation and vol. Its central argument is contrarian for a gold house: a 1970s-style second inflation wave is possible but would NOT automatically produce a gold rally, because a faster-reacting Fed would deliver tighter policy and slower growth; gold's real supports are central bank buying and Asian demand, plus the eventual fall in long-dated yields when 'something breaks'.

insights.claim: Gold finished July 2026 unchanged at US$4,027/oz after repeatedly testing the US$4,000 level, leaving it down 7.8% year-to-date in US dollars.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: US$4,000 is the level being defended repeatedly — a clean technical line for adding or cutting gold exposure.
insights.quote: Gold finished July practically where it started, at US$4,027/oz, having tested the US$4,000 level on several occasions during the month
insights.locator: Unmoved

insights.claim: The World Gold Council's Gold Returns Attribution Model attributes July 2026's flat gold price to positive momentum factors offsetting a fall in risk factors (breakeven inflation and implied volatility), with rising yields (opportunity cost IR) roughly cancelled out by a falling US dollar (opportunity cost FX).
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: A flat print masks offsetting drivers — if the dollar stops falling while yields keep rising, the rate drag stops being neutralised.
insights.locator: Our monthly Gold Returns Attribution Model (GRAM)

insights.claim: The World Gold Council treats sharp falls in the gold price as often reversed in a subsequent period, making momentum a mean-reversion factor rather than a trend-following one in its attribution model.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: Implies a systematic dip-buying tailwind after gold drawdowns — relevant after a -8% y-t-d move.
insights.quote: Sharp falls in gold prices are often reversed in a subsequent period
insights.locator: Our monthly Gold Returns Attribution Model (GRAM)

insights.claim: GRAM is a multiple regression of monthly gold returns on four thematic driver categories — economic expansion, risk & uncertainty, opportunity cost, and momentum — estimated over a rolling five-year period, and it treats investment demand as the marginal driver of gold price returns in the short run.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: A reusable decomposition for judging whether a gold move is rate-driven, fear-driven, or just flow/momentum — and therefore whether it persists.
insights.quote: These themes capture motives behind gold demand; most importantly, investment demand, which is considered the marginal driver of gold price returns in the short run.
insights.locator: Chart 1 footnote / GRAM description

insights.claim: Gold returns in July 2026 stayed within a +/-2% band across all ten major currencies, ranging from -2.0% in JPY terms to +1.9% in TRY, but year-to-date dispersion is wide: -12.0% in AUD versus +7.3% in INR and +2.0% in TRY.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: Currency of denomination has been worth ~19 points of return y-t-d — hedged versus unhedged gold exposure is the bigger decision than gold itself this year.
insights.locator: Table 1: Gold within a +/-2% return range

insights.claim: Gold's record high of US$5,405/oz was set on 29 January 2026, meaning the metal ended July 2026 roughly 25% below its all-time peak, with EUR, JPY and GBP records set slightly later on 2 March 2026.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: Frames 2026 as a post-blowoff consolidation year, not a bull market — sizing gold as a drawdown recovery trade rather than momentum chase.
insights.locator: Table 1: Record high price / Record high date

themes.theme: European ETF bid against 15-year-high real bund yields

insights.claim: Gold ETF flows were positive in July 2026 with European funds leading, even though real bund yields sat at 15-year highs — breaking the historical pattern in which European gold investors shun the metal in positive real rate environments.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: A behavioural regime change in the largest incremental Western buyer; if it persists, gold's negative real-rate beta is weakening and the metal can rally without a rate cut.
insights.quote: European gold investors have historically shunned gold in positive real rate environments and inflows in July arrived against a backdrop of real bund yields at 15-year highs.
insights.locator: Positive ETF flows supported gold in July

insights.claim: The World Gold Council cannot yet distinguish whether July's European gold ETF inflows reflect regional rotation out of equities or simply an attractive entry price after gold's decline.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: Watch European equity outflows alongside gold ETF creations — if the two co-move, the bid is structural allocation, not opportunistic dip-buying.
insights.quote: It is unclear whether regional rotation out of equities or simply just an attractive price point were core drivers.
insights.locator: Positive ETF flows supported gold in July

themes.theme: Second-wave inflation risk and its new sources

insights.claim: The most useful lesson from Apollo Asset Management's much-discussed 1970s inflation analogy is not the oil parallel but the observation that inflation arrives in waves, because once an initial shock changes behaviour and expectations a second wave becomes more likely.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: Reframes disinflation prints as a pause rather than an all-clear — argues for keeping inflation-hedge optionality on even as CPI cools.
insights.quote: The more interesting parallel is not oil, but the possibility that inflation arrives in waves. Once an inflation shock changes behaviour and expectations, a second wave can become more likely.
insights.locator: Making waves

insights.claim: The next inflation shock is more likely to originate in strategic stockpiling and competition for critical resources — funded by both government and corporate AI spending — than in oil embargoes, because unions are weaker, oil matters less and the Fed has a clearer inflation mandate than in the 1970s.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: Points the inflation hedge at critical minerals and industrial commodities tied to AI/datacentre and strategic-reserve buildouts, not energy.
insights.quote: This time, the risk may come less from oil embargoes and more from strategic stockpiling and competition for critical resources fuelled by both government and corporate spending (AI).
insights.locator: Why inflation could come back in force

insights.claim: The Federal Reserve's 'on hold' strategy is failing on the World Gold Council's read of the fed funds rate, core PCE and unemployment through July 2026, with the US-Iran War marked as a shock during the hold period.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: If the hold is judged a policy error, the market reprices toward a later, sharper tightening — bearish duration, initially bearish gold.
insights.quote: The Fed’s ‘on hold’ strategy isn’t working
insights.locator: Chart 3 title

insights.claim: Year-ahead inflation expectations in the University of Michigan survey are rising even among Republican respondents, removing the partisan-distortion excuse that has been used to dismiss the survey since the US presidential election.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: Broad-based expectation drift is what forces a central bank's hand — a leading indicator for a hawkish Fed pivot.
insights.quote: Even Republicans are upping their forecasts
insights.locator: Chart 4 title

insights.claim: US firms are passing higher costs through to customers, evidenced by the average of three Federal Reserve regional banks' prices-received series and the NFIB small-business higher-prices index.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: Pass-through, not just input costs, is the transmission channel into CPI — these surveys lead headline prints.
insights.quote: Firms are passing on higher costs
insights.locator: Chart 5 title

insights.claim: Near-term disinflation cannot be ruled out precisely because the underlying US economy is not as robust as it was after COVID when inflation last hit, so cracks could easily appear.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: The bear case for the inflation trade is growth failure, not supply normalisation — hedge inflation exposure with recession-sensitive duration.
insights.quote: the underlying US economy – and elsewhere - isn’t as robust as it was after COVID when inflation last hit and cracks could easily appear, but upside inflation risks are stacking up
insights.locator: Why inflation could come back in force

insights.claim: With US core inflation at 3.3%, markets are edging toward the level at which investors begin to view inflation as unruly rather than benign.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: 3.3% is roughly 0.7pp below the ~4% threshold where the article says gold's inflation sensitivity switches on — a specific trigger level to monitor.
insights.quote: With US core inflation at 3.3%, we are edging towards levels where investors may start to view inflation as a little more unruly.
insights.locator: So it seems that the case for higher inflation is there

insights.claim: Gold is largely insensitive to benign inflation and only responds meaningfully once inflation exceeds roughly 4%, at which point it reads as a policy mistake — the same dynamic seen post-COVID.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: Do not buy gold on a drift from 2% to 3% inflation; the payoff is a threshold option struck near 4%.
insights.quote: When inflation is benign, gold doesn't really pay attention. But above 4%, it starts to feel like a policy mistake, as we saw post COVID.
insights.locator: Gold and inflation, not joined at the hip

insights.claim: In a quarterly regression from Q1 1971 to Q2 2026, the coefficient on the change in US CPI for gold returns more than doubles from 1.32 in the full 222-observation sample to 2.98 (10% significance) in the 72-observation subsample where inflation exceeds 4%.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: Quantifies the regime switch: gold's inflation beta roughly doubles above 4%, so option-like sizing beats linear exposure.
insights.locator: Table 2: Inflation starts to matter when it’s high

insights.claim: The US dollar is the only variable statistically significant at the 1% level in both regimes of the World Gold Council's gold-return regression, with a coefficient of -0.93 in the full sample and -1.2 in the high-inflation subsample, versus a statistically weaker real fed funds coefficient of -0.63 / -0.84.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: DXY, not real rates or CPI, is the most reliable single driver to trade gold against — and its sensitivity strengthens when inflation is high.
insights.locator: Table 2: Inflation starts to matter when it’s high

insights.claim: Inflation alone will not lift gold; the strong catalyst requires inflation accelerating past the threshold while real rates fall, the dollar weakens or recession risks rise simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: A gold long predicated purely on a CPI upside surprise is mis-specified — the trade needs the dollar or real rates to break the same way.
insights.quote: Should inflation accelerate beyond those levels while real rates fall, the dollar weaken or recession risks rise, it could prove a much stronger catalyst for gold investment.
insights.locator: That doesn't mean inflation automatically translates

insights.claim: The World Gold Council explicitly rejects a late-1970s-style second inflation wave, arguing today's Fed has shown a fervent distaste for inflation — citing Warsh vowing to crush it — so a renewed inflation surge would produce tighter policy and slower growth rather than a classic inflation breakout.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: Contrarian for a gold publisher: it argues against the standard 'inflation wave equals gold moonshot' trade and toward a growth-scare trade instead.
insights.quote: a renewed inflation surge could produce tighter policy and slower growth rather than a classic 1970s-style inflation breakout
insights.locator: But will we have a second wave like in the late 1970s?

insights.claim: Today's US consumer is less able to absorb a sustained rise in prices than in the 1970s because the personal savings rate is at 2.8% of disposable income, not far from all-time lows.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: A 2.8% savings buffer means an inflation shock converts quickly into demand destruction — shortens the inflation trade's half-life and favours defensives.
insights.quote: today's consumer is arguably less able to absorb a sustained rise in prices, with the personal savings rate not far from all-time-lows
insights.locator: But will we have a second wave like in the late 1970s?

insights.claim: Inflation is looking increasingly problematic but a repeat of the late 1970s remains highly unlikely even if the Federal Reserve commits another misstep on the scale of 2022, with tighter policy and slower growth the more probable path.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: Positions the base case as stagflation-lite resolving into a growth slowdown — favour duration on weakness over commodity beta.
insights.quote: inflation is looking increasingly problematic, but a repeat of the late 1970s still seems highly unlikely even if the Fed has another misstep like in 2022
insights.locator: In summary

themes.theme: Central banks and Asia as the structural bid

insights.claim: US inflation is no longer the dominant driver of gold, because central banks and Asian investors have become increasingly important sources of demand that may behave independently of US macro factors.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: US CPI and Fed models will systematically under-predict gold; monitor official-sector purchase data and Asian consumer demand as the marginal price setters.
insights.quote: And, of course, US inflation is no longer the only tune to which gold dances.
insights.locator: And, of course, US inflation is no longer

insights.claim: Gold has performed impressively despite historically restrictive US real rates since 2023, with the US 10-year TIPS yield in restrictive territory while the gold price rose — attributed largely to central bank and Asian demand rather than Western rate-sensitive flows.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: Breaks the classic short-gold-on-rising-real-yields rule; the negative TIPS correlation trade has been structurally impaired since 2023.
insights.quote: gold has performed impressively despite historically restrictive US real rates since 2023 - largely thanks to these two sources of demand
insights.locator: Chart 7: Elevated real rates have not been an obstacle

insights.claim: The near-term path for gold is higher yields and some price pressure while markets test the Federal Reserve's resolve, but eventually inflation, growth or both break, longer-dated yields start moving lower, and that combined with continued central bank buying and Asian consumer demand becomes supportive.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: Sequencing matters: pain first, then the bid — argues for scaling into gold on the yield-driven drawdown rather than chasing.
insights.quote: But if history is any guide, something eventually breaks: inflation, growth, or both. At that point, longer-dated yields are likely to start moving lower.
insights.locator: In summary

insights.claim: The World Gold Council expects the eventual gold recovery to be supportive but explicitly not a repeat of the outsized gains of 2025.
insights.speaker: Johan Palmberg
insights.so_what: A gold-industry body capping its own upside expectation is a meaningful sentiment signal — size return assumptions to single-digit/low-double-digit, not 2025-style.
insights.quote: albeit without necessarily repeating the outsized gains of 2025
insights.locator: In summary
